To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the transfusion history and the frequency of alloimmunization were significantly different in Jamaican and UK patients with homozyggous sickle cell anemia.
the proportion of patients transfusioned, number of units transfusioned and frequency of red-cell antibodies are significantly greater in the UK than in Jamaica.
the proportion of Jamaicans transfused did not significantly differ from the UK group, although the number of red cell antibodies was significantly greater in the UK group.

the development of new methods of diagnosis and treatment of sickle cell disease.

the epidemiology of sickle cell disease and its associated complications, the pathophysiological and molecular basis of the complications of sickle cell anaemia, and the development of strategies for the prevention, treatment and management of these complications.
the development and evaluation of novel therapies for sickle cell disease (SCD) with the ultimate aim of reducing the burden of disease in affected individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Jamaican and the UK populations are not comparable.
Jamaican patients have a lower frequency of alloimmunization than UK patients, probably reflecting the greater frequency and volume of transfusion in the UK.
Jamaicans have a lower frequency of alloantibodies and are more likely to be alloimmunized by transfusion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transfusion history and the incidence of red cell antibodies are significantly different in patients with homo­zygous sick­le cell disease in Jamaica compared with the United Kingdom.
there is no significant difference in the transfusion history of Jamaican and UK patients, although the frequency of alloimmunization is significantly greater in the latter.
there is no significant difference between the Jamaican and UK patients with regards to transfusion history.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the frequency of red blood cell (RBC) alloantibodies in Jamaican subjects is low compared to the frequency in UK patients.

the frequency of alloimmunization in sickle cell disease is related to the frequency of transfusion and that the frequency of red-cell antibodies in sickle cell patients in the United Kingdom is higher than in Jamaica.
the Jamaican cohort is a good resource to study the natural history of SS disease and the impact of transfusion.
